scenes.tts: A newborn neuron must cross a wall many times its own size. It has no legs. How does it get across?
scenes.visual: Cross-section of the developing cortical wall. A neuron drawn to scale beside it, labelled: about 10 micrometres across.
scenes.narration: A newborn neuron must cross a wall many times its own size. It has no legs. How does it get across?

scenes.tts: The wall has layers. Neurons are born in the ventricular zone, on the inside. Next come the subventricular and intermediate zones.
scenes.visual: The wall builds one zone at a time from the ventricle outward, each labelled: ventricular zone, subventricular zone, intermediate zone.
scenes.narration: The wall has layers. Neurons are born in the ventricular zone, on the inside. Next come the subventricular and intermediate zones.

scenes.tts: Then the cortical plate, where neurons settle. The marginal zone sits on top, just under the surface.
scenes.visual: Two more zones appear and are labelled: cortical plate, marginal zone. The pial surface is marked at the top.
scenes.narration: Then the cortical plate, where neurons settle. The marginal zone sits on top, just under the surface.

scenes.tts: A neuron's birth date predicts its layer. Early-born neurons settle deep, later-born ones nearer the surface. So every neuron must travel.
scenes.visual: Neurons coloured by birth date settle in the cortical plate, early-born deep and later-born above. An arrow runs from the ventricular zone up to the cortical plate.
scenes.narration: A neuron's birth date predicts its layer. Early-born neurons settle deep, later-born ones nearer the surface. So every neuron must travel.

scenes.tts: A migrating neuron has a leading process, one long arm pointing the way. Behind it is the cell body, which holds the nucleus.
scenes.visual: A bipolar neuron, labelled: leading process, cell body (soma), nucleus as an outlined disc.
scenes.narration: A migrating neuron has a leading process, one long arm pointing the way. Behind it is the cell body, which holds the nucleus.

scenes.tts: Near the nucleus sits the centrosome, the cell's main organizing centre for microtubules.
scenes.visual: A bright dot beside the nucleus, labelled: centrosome. Faint microtubules radiate from it.
scenes.narration: Near the nucleus sits the centrosome, the cell's main organizing centre for microtubules.

scenes.tts: In nineteen seventy-two, Pasko Rakic rebuilt young neurons from fetal monkey cortex. He found them pressed along fibres of radial glee-uh, long cells spanning the wall.
scenes.caption: In 1972, Pasko Rakic rebuilt young neurons from fetal monkey cortex. He found them pressed along fibres of radial glia, long cells spanning the wall.
scenes.visual: Credit card: Rakic, 1972, serial electron micrographs, fetal rhesus monkey cortex. Radial glial fibres span the wall; neurons lie pressed along them at many depths.
scenes.narration: In 1972, Pasko Rakic rebuilt young neurons from fetal monkey cortex. He found them pressed along fibres of radial glia, long cells spanning the wall.

scenes.tts: But fixed tissue shows contact. It cannot show which cell moved, or how.
scenes.visual: The same image, frozen, with a label: fixed tissue shows contact, not motion.
scenes.narration: But fixed tissue shows contact. It cannot show which cell moved, or how.

scenes.tts: In nineteen eighty-seven, James Edmondson and Mary Hatten filmed living neurons moving on glial fibres in a dish.
scenes.caption: In 1987, James Edmondson and Mary Hatten filmed living neurons moving on glial fibres in a dish.
scenes.visual: Credit card: Edmondson and Hatten, 1987, granule neurons and astroglia from early postnatal mouse cerebellum, on a coverslip.
scenes.narration: In 1987, James Edmondson and Mary Hatten filmed living neurons moving on glial fibres in a dish.

scenes.tts: The neurons moved in a stop-and-go rhythm. The tip reached forward and pulled back, out of step with the cell body.
scenes.visual: Time-lapse: a neuron advances along a fibre in jumps. Its tip extends and retracts on its own schedule while the soma waits, then jumps.
scenes.narration: The neurons moved in a stop-and-go rhythm. The tip reached forward and pulled back, out of step with the cell body.

scenes.tts: Bruce Schaar and Susan McConnell then watched single cycles in neuroblasts, young migrating neurons, from newborn rats. These are not cortical neurons.
scenes.visual: Credit card: Schaar and McConnell, 2005, anterior subventricular-zone neuroblasts of newborn rats, migrating in a gel. Small label: not cortical neurons.
scenes.narration: Bruce Schaar and Susan McConnell then watched single cycles in neuroblasts, young migrating neurons, from newborn rats. These are not cortical neurons.

scenes.tts: A swelling forms in the leading process, ahead of the nucleus. Which moves into it first, the centrosome or the nucleus?
scenes.visual: A swelling bulges in the leading process ahead of the nucleus. The centrosome dot and the nucleus disc both wait. Caption: Pause and predict.
scenes.narration: A swelling forms in the leading process, ahead of the nucleus. Which moves into it first, the centrosome or the nucleus?

scenes.tts: The centrosome goes first. Cells fixed at this moment show it ahead, and later movies of cortical neurons tracked it. Then the nucleus jumps forward.
scenes.visual: The dot moves into the swelling; a beat; then the disc jumps forward into it. Labels: stroke one, stroke two. Small note: centrosome position from cells fixed mid-cycle; later tracked live in rat cortical slices. The cycle repeats.
scenes.narration: The centrosome goes first. Cells fixed at this moment show it ahead, and later movies of cortical neurons tracked it. Then the nucleus jumps forward.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea. In the typical bipolar climb, the front goes first. The cell has moved only when its nucleus catches up.
scenes.visual: On screen: Typical bipolar climb. The front goes first. The cell has moved only when its nucleus catches up.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea. In the typical bipolar climb, the front goes first. The cell has moved only when its nucleus catches up.

scenes.tts: A tip can keep growing while the nucleus stays put. So track the nucleus against the tissue, not the tip.
scenes.visual: Two neurons side by side against a fixed grid of tissue. In one, the tip grows while the disc stays still; a cross marks it: not migration.
scenes.narration: A tip can keep growing while the nucleus stays put. So track the nucleus against the tissue, not the tip.

scenes.tts: Count the steps of the nucleus. Six micrometres a step, four steps an hour, gives twenty-four micrometres an hour.
scenes.visual: A ruler and a clock in the corner. On screen: 6 micrometres per step x 4 steps an hour = 24 micrometres an hour, measured at the nucleus.
scenes.narration: Count the steps of the nucleus. 6 micrometres a step, 4 steps an hour, gives 24 micrometres an hour.
scenes.caption: Count the steps of the nucleus. 6 micrometres a step, 4 steps an hour, gives 24 micrometres an hour.

scenes.tts: Follow the nucleus, not the tip.
scenes.visual: Closing card: Follow the nucleus, not the tip.
scenes.narration: Follow the nucleus, not the tip.
